java.say: First the program makes the real answer key. It knows the answer to each question.
Then it makes a proxy for a student. The proxy keeps the real answer key in its field `real`, and remembers that this user is not a teacher.
And a second proxy for a teacher, in front of the same real answer key.
The student asks for the answer to question 1. The variable has the type AnswerKey, so the program cannot see that a proxy stands in front of the real object.
The proxy gets the call first and checks the access. This user is not a teacher, so it returns "No access". The real answer key is never called.
Now the teacher asks the same question, through the other proxy.
The proxy checks the access again. This user is a teacher, so the check passes.
The proxy passes the call on to the real answer key.

java.at: public String answer(int question) { return answers.get(question); }
java.say: The real answer key looks up the answer: "B". It does not know about the access check.
The proxy returns "B" as it is. A proxy does not change the result.
The program prints B. The interface and the real answer key did not change; the only new part is the proxy in between.
